conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Sarah, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived.

We’ll use a quick, 10-item questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It simply asks how you’ve felt in the past week—no right or wrong answers. Everything you share is confidential and helps us understand what kind of support or resources might help you feel more like yourself again.

Whenever you’re ready, we can start with the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

Hi, Sarah.  
Um… I guess I can still laugh a little—like if my partner shows me a silly meme—but it feels kind of forced. Mostly I’m just worn out, so the “funny side” doesn’t come naturally right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes I can laugh a little—maybe if my partner makes a joke—but it doesn’t come easily. Most of the time I’m too tired or pre-occupied with the baby.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really, honestly. Even little things I used to enjoy—like watching a favorite show or grabbing coffee—feel more like chores than treats. I’ll think, “That could be nice,” but the excitement just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… sometimes I catch myself doing that. Like if the baby won’t settle, I’ll think maybe I’m not doing something right or I’m not good at this mom thing. I know in my head it’s probably not true, but the thought still pops up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do get those waves of worry, even when everything seems okay. Like I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s breathing fine, and suddenly I’m checking the monitor every two minutes or imagining something bad might happen. There isn’t really a reason—it just shows up and my chest feels tight until I distract myself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times I’ve had that sudden rush—heart pounding, can’t catch my breath—like I’m about to bolt out of the room, even though nothing’s wrong. It passes pretty quickly, maybe a minute or two, but it leaves me shaky and wondering what just happened.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll start one chore, the baby cries, and suddenly it’s noon and I haven’t eaten or brushed my teeth. I keep thinking, “I should be able to handle this,” but it piles up and I just feel… swamped.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m miserable, but I do feel low enough that my mind keeps spinning once the lights are off. I’ll lie there listening to every baby grunt, replaying the day, worrying I forgot something important. Takes me ages to drift off, and then I wake up at the slightest sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time, not every moment—like when the baby smiles it lifts me for a second—but kind of an overall gloom that sits on my chest. It’s hard to explain; things just feel heavy and gray more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I’ve teared up once or twice—mostly when I’m extra tired—but full-on crying hasn’t happened. I feel kind of numb or flat more than weepy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I don’t want to hurt myself—I just want to feel like me again.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 20: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS-based interview):

1. Anhedonia: marked reduction in ability to experience pleasure or anticipate enjoyment  
2. Low/“flat” mood described as “overall gloom” most of the day  
3. Excessive self-blame and doubts about maternal competence  
4. Unprompted anxiety and catastrophic worry; occasional brief panic episodes (palpitations, breathlessness)  
5. Perceives daily demands as “swamped” and “treading water”  
6. Initial insomnia linked to ruminating and hyper-vigilance about infant  
7. Episodic tearfulness but no frank crying spells  
8. Denies any self-harm ideation

Risk indicators  
- Persistent mood and anxiety symptoms beyond two-week benchmark  
- Functional impact: impaired sleep, concentration, task completion  
- No suicidal thoughts or intent (safety factor negative)

Screening impression  
Responses are consistent with probable postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; score suggests moderate clinical concern. Continue monitoring, consider formal assessment for PPD/PPA and psychosocial supports; safety reassessment if any worsening or emergent self-harm thoughts.
